lessons.title: Why Prune Tomatoes: Benefits and Timing
lessons.body:
Pruning tomatoes is not about making the plant look neat. It is about directing the plant's energy into fruit instead of leaves and stems you cannot sell. On a typical African smallholding, an unpruned indeterminate tomato plant can grow into a tangled bush 2 metres wide, with fruit hidden under leaves, ripening slowly and rotting before you pick it. Pruning opens the canopy so sunlight hits the fruit and air moves through, which cuts fungal diseases like early blight and leaf mould by half or more. It also makes spraying, weeding, and harvesting faster because you can see what you are doing.

The best time to start pruning is when the plant is 30â45 cm tall, usually 3â4 weeks after transplanting. At that stage, you can clearly see the main stem and the side shoots (suckers) that grow in the leaf axilsâthe V-shaped joint between the main stem and a leaf. Remove suckers when they are 5â10 cm long, snapping them off with your thumb and forefinger or cutting with clean secateurs. Do this in the morning after dew has dried, so wounds heal quickly. Never prune when plants are wet; that spreads disease.

Prune little and often, every 5â7 days, rather than one heavy session. For determinate (bush) varieties, pruning is minimalâjust remove leaves touching the soil. For indeterminate (vining) types, remove all suckers below the first flower cluster, then decide whether to keep one, two, or three main stems. In hot, dry areas like northern Nigeria or Senegal, keep more leaves to shade fruit from sunscald. In humid areas like Uganda or Cameroon, prune more aggressively for airflow.

Stop pruning when the plant has set 4â6 trusses of fruit or when 30 days remain before you expect the crop to finish. Late pruning removes leaves that are feeding the ripening fruit and reduces yield. Always disinfect your secateurs or knife with methylated spirits or bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) between plants to prevent spreading bacterial wilt and mosaic virus. With consistent pruning, you can expect 20â30% more marketable fruit and easier disease control.

lessons.title: Suckering and Removing Lower Leaves
lessons.body:
Suckering is the single most important pruning job on indeterminate tomatoes. A sucker is a new shoot that grows from the leaf axilâthe point where a leaf joins the main stem. If left, each sucker becomes a full branch with its own leaves and flowers, turning one plant into a jungle. For a farmer selling tomatoes, that means smaller fruit, more disease, and back-breaking harvests. Remove suckers when they are small, 5â10 cm, by pinching them out with your thumb and forefinger. If they are bigger, use a sharp, clean knife or secateurs. Work in the morning, not when plants are wet.

Start suckering 3â4 weeks after transplanting, when the first flower cluster appears. Remove all suckers below that first cluster. Above it, you choose a training system. For a single-stem (cordon) system, remove every sucker. For a two-stem system, keep the sucker just below the first flower cluster and remove all others. For three stems, keep two strong suckers. Two-stem systems are popular in Kenya and Tanzania because they give more fruit per plant without needing extra stakes. Check plants every 5â7 days; suckers grow fast in warm, wet weather.

Removing lower leaves is the second key job. Once fruit on the first truss is full size and starting to ripen, remove all leaves below that truss. These leaves are old, shaded, and often diseased. They also touch the soil and splash rain onto fruit, causing early blight and fruit rot. Cut them off cleanly with secateurs, leaving a small stub. Do this graduallyâno more than 3 leaves per plant per weekâso the plant does not go into shock. In humid regions, remove leaves up to 30 cm above the ground to improve airflow.

Never remove leaves above a ripening truss; they are needed for photosynthesis and to shade fruit from sunscald. In very hot, dry areas, keep more leaves. Dispose of all removed leaves and suckers away from the fieldâdo not compost them if disease is present. Burn or bury them. Clean your tools between plants with bleach solution. With proper suckering and leaf removal, your plants will produce larger, cleaner fruit and you will spray less.

lessons.title: Staking, Caging, and Trellising Methods
lessons.body:
Tomato plants that are left to sprawl on the ground produce less fruit and more rot. Staking, caging, or trellising lifts the plant and fruit off the soil, improving airflow, reducing disease, and making harvest faster. The method you choose depends on your variety, budget, and market. For determinate (bush) tomatoes, a simple cage or short stake works. For indeterminate (vining) types, you need a strong trellis because plants can grow 2 metres or more.

Staking is the cheapest method. Use wooden stakes or bamboo poles 1.5â2 metres long and 3â5 cm thick. Drive them 30 cm into the ground at transplanting time, 10â15 cm from the plant, to avoid root damage. As the plant grows, tie the main stem to the stake every 20â30 cm using soft twine or strips of old cloth. Tie in a figure-eight loop so the stem does not rub against the stake. In windy areas, use a stake that is taller than the plant and drive it deeper. Staking works best for single-stem trained plants.

Caging uses a cylinder of wire mesh (concrete reinforcement mesh with 15 cm squares works well) about 45 cm in diameter and 1.2â1.5 metres tall. Place the cage over the young plant and let it grow inside. Cages are fast, need no tying, and support the whole plant. They are ideal for determinate varieties and for farmers near cities who can buy mesh. A cage costs more upfront but lasts 5â10 years.

Trellising is the best method for indeterminate tomatoes in Africa. Use the âbush trellisâ or âstake and weaveâ system: drive strong wooden posts every 3â4 metres along the row, 2 metres tall. Run a wire or strong rope along the top of the posts. Then, as plants grow, weave twine between plants and around the wire, or use the Florida Weave (see next lesson). In areas with strong winds, use a diagonal brace at the ends. Trellising keeps fruit clean, reduces foliar disease by 40â60%, and makes picking 2â3 times faster. Always use clean, UV-resistant twine; ordinary string rots in one season. Inspect and repair trellises weekly.

lessons.title: String Trellis and Florida Weave Techniques
lessons.body:
String trellis and Florida Weave are two low-cost, high-efficiency methods for supporting indeterminate tomatoes. They are popular in commercial tomato production across Africa because they use cheap materials and can be built quickly. Both methods lift plants off the ground, improving airflow and reducing fruit rot. They also make harvesting easier because fruit hangs at waist height.

String trellis (also called âvertical stringâ or âcordonâ system) uses a horizontal wire or rope strung between strong posts at 2â2.5 metres high. For each plant, tie a piece of UV-resistant twine to the top wire and let it hang down. As the plant grows, gently twist the main stem around the string, or tie it loosely with soft twine every 20â30 cm. Remove all suckers so the plant grows as a single stem up the string. When the plant reaches the top wire, pinch out the growing tip to stop it. This method gives the highest fruit quality because every leaf gets sun and air. It is ideal for greenhouses and open fields with little wind. Use 1 string per plant; for a 100-plant plot, you need about 200 metres of twine and 20 posts.

Florida Weave is faster and cheaper for field production. You need stakes every 3â4 metres along the row, 1.5â2 metres tall. Run a strong wire or rope along the top of the stakes. Then, starting when plants are 30â40 cm tall, weave twine between the plants: tie the twine to the first stake, pass it in front of the first plant, behind the second, in front of the third, and so on. On the return pass, do the opposite: behind the first, in front of the second. This creates a figure-eight that holds the plants upright. Add a new weave every 20â30 cm of growth, usually every 7â10 days. Use two or three weaves per season. Florida Weave works for determinate and indeterminate types, but indeterminate plants may need a top wire for extra support.

Both methods cost less than individual stakes. For 100 plants, string trellis costs about $15â20 for twine and wire; Florida Weave costs about $10â15. Always use UV-stabilised twine; cheap string breaks after 2â3 months. Check and tighten weaves after heavy rain or wind. Remove and burn old twine at seasonâs end to reduce disease carryover.

lessons.title: Managing Determinate vs Indeterminate Growth
lessons.body:
Tomato varieties are either determinate or indeterminate, and your pruning and training must match the type. Determinate (bush) tomatoes grow to a fixed height, usually 60â120 cm, then stop and put all energy into fruit that ripens within 2â3 weeks. Indeterminate (vining) tomatoes keep growing and producing fruit until frost or disease stops them; they can reach 2â3 metres in a season. Knowing which you have saves you from wasting time on the wrong pruning.

Determinate tomatoes need very little pruning. Do not remove suckers above the first flower cluster; those suckers produce most of your fruit. Only remove leaves that touch the soil and any diseased leaves. Stake or cage determinate plants to keep fruit off the ground, but do not train them to a single stemâthat reduces yield. Common determinate varieties in Africa include âRoma VFâ, âUC82Bâ, and âTanyaâ. They are good for farmers who want a concentrated harvest for market or processing.

Indeterminate tomatoes need regular suckering and training. Remove all suckers below the first flower cluster. Above it, choose a system: single stem (remove all suckers), two stems (keep one sucker just below the first flower cluster), or three stems (keep two suckers). Two-stem systems are popular in Kenya and Tanzania for open-field production because they balance yield and airflow. Indeterminate varieties include âMoney Makerâ, âAnna F1â, âPadmaâ, and âCobraâ. They produce fruit over many months, so you need a strong trellis.

In hot, dry areas like northern Nigeria or Senegal, indeterminate plants benefit from more leaves for shade. Prune less aggressivelyâkeep three stems and remove only lower leaves. In humid areas like Uganda or Cameroon, prune more aggressively to one or two stems to reduce fungal disease. For determinate types in any region, avoid heavy pruning; it shocks the plant and reduces the concentrated harvest.

Finally, plan your season. Determinate types are good for a quick crop before rains end. Indeterminate types need a longer season and steady management. Always check the seed label or ask your supplier. If unsure, observe: if the plant stops growing and flowers all at once, it is determinate. If it keeps growing and flowering, it is indeterminate. Match your pruning to the type and you will get the most from every plant.

lessons.title: Pruning for Disease Prevention and Airflow
lessons.body:
Disease is the biggest threat to tomato farming in Africa. Fungal diseases like early blight, late blight, and leaf mould thrive in still, humid air and on leaves that stay wet. Pruning is your first line of defence. By removing excess leaves and opening the canopy, you let sunlight and wind dry the plant quickly, cutting disease pressure by half or more. You also remove infected leaves before they spread spores to healthy parts.

Start by removing all leaves that touch the soil. Soil-borne fungi like Fusarium and Verticillium wilt enter through wounded lower leaves. Cut these off cleanly with secateurs, leaving a 2â3 cm stub. Do this when plants are dry, ideally mid-morning. Remove any leaf with spots, yellowing, or mould immediately. Put diseased leaves in a plastic bag and remove them from the fieldâdo not compost them. Burn or bury them deep. After handling diseased plants, wash your hands and disinfect tools with bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) or methylated spirits.

Airflow is critical. For indeterminate tomatoes, train plants to a single or double stem and tie them to a trellis. This keeps leaves separated and allows wind to pass through. Remove suckers regularlyâevery 5â7 daysâbecause dense suckers create a humid microclimate inside the plant. In humid regions, remove leaves up to 30 cm above the ground and any leaves shading fruit. But do not over-prune: leaves are the plantâs food factory. A good rule is to remove no more than 3 leaves per plant per week. Over-pruning causes sunscald, small fruit, and reduced yield.

Pruning also helps with pest control. Removing lower leaves makes it harder for whiteflies, aphids, and spider mites to hide. It also improves spray coverageâwhen you spray fungicide or insecticide, the droplets reach more of the plant. Always prune before spraying, not after, so wounds are not exposed to chemicals.

Finally, keep a clean field. Remove pruned material immediately. Do not leave it between rows. Use a 2-year rotation with non-solanaceous crops like maize or beans. Choose resistant varieties when available. With consistent pruning for airflow and disease removal, you can reduce fungicide sprays by 30â50% and harvest more marketable fruit.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of pruning tomato plants?
options: A) To make the plant look neat
B) To direct energy into fruit and improve airflow
C) To reduce the number of flowers
D) To make the plant grow taller
quiz.explanation: Pruning directs the plant's energy into fruit production and opens the canopy for better airflow and sunlight.

quiz.q: When should you start pruning tomato plants?
options: B) When plants are 30â45 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Starting at 30â45 cm tall allows you to clearly see the main stem and suckers.

quiz.q: What is a sucker on a tomato plant?
options: B) A shoot growing from the leaf axil
C) A root growing above ground
quiz.explanation: A sucker is a new shoot that grows from the leaf axil, the joint between the main stem and a leaf.

quiz.q: How often should you remove suckers from indeterminate tomatoes?
options: C) Only at the end of the season
quiz.explanation: Suckers grow fast, so checking and removing them every 5â7 days keeps plants manageable.

quiz.q: Why should you disinfect pruning tools between plants?
options: A) To make them last longer
B) To prevent spreading diseases like bacterial wilt
quiz.explanation: Disinfecting tools prevents the spread of pathogens from one plant to another.

quiz.q: When removing lower leaves, how many leaves per plant per week is safe?
options: C) All leaves below the first truss at once
D) None; never remove lower leaves
quiz.explanation: Removing more than 3 leaves per week can shock the plant and reduce yield.

quiz.q: Which training method is best for indeterminate tomatoes in Africa?
options: A) Letting them sprawl on the ground
B) Staking with a single stake
C) Trellising with a stake and weave system
quiz.explanation: Trellising with a stake and weave system provides strong support for tall indeterminate plants.

quiz.q: What is the ideal height for stakes used in staking tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Stakes of 1.5â2 metres support indeterminate tomatoes that can grow 2 metres or more.

quiz.q: How deep should you drive a stake into the ground?
quiz.explanation: Driving stakes 30 cm deep provides stability without damaging the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using cages for tomatoes?
options: A) They are the cheapest method
B) They require no tying and support the whole plant
C) They are best for indeterminate varieties
quiz.explanation: Cages support the entire plant without needing to tie stems, and they last several years.

quiz.q: In the string trellis method, what do you do as the plant grows?
options: A) Let it sprawl on the ground
B) Twist the main stem around the string
quiz.explanation: Twisting the main stem around the string supports the plant and keeps it growing upward.

quiz.q: How often should you add a new weave in the Florida Weave system?
options: C) Only at the end of the season
quiz.explanation: Adding a weave every 20â30 cm of growth keeps plants upright as they grow.

quiz.q: Which type of twine is best for trellising tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: UV-resistant twine lasts longer and does not rot quickly in the sun and rain.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between determinate and indeterminate tomatoes?
options: A) Determinate grow to a fixed height and fruit ripens all at once
B) Indeterminate stop growing after first fruit
D) Indeterminate are always bush type
quiz.explanation: Determinate tomatoes grow to a fixed height and produce a concentrated harvest.

quiz.q: How should you prune determinate tomatoes?
options: B) Remove only leaves touching the soil and diseased leaves
C) Train to a single stem
quiz.explanation: Determinate tomatoes need minimal pruning; removing suckers reduces yield.

quiz.q: Which of these is an indeterminate tomato variety?
quiz.explanation: Money Maker is a common indeterminate variety that continues growing and fruiting.

quiz.q: In hot, dry areas, how should you adjust pruning for indeterminate tomatoes?
options: A) Prune more aggressively to one stem
B) Keep more leaves for shade
D) Do not prune at all
quiz.explanation: Keeping more leaves helps shade fruit and prevent sunscald in hot, dry conditions.

quiz.q: Why is airflow important in tomato plants?
options: A) It helps plants grow taller
B) It reduces fungal diseases by drying leaves
quiz.explanation: Good airflow dries leaves quickly, reducing the humidity that fungal diseases need.

quiz.q: What should you do with diseased leaves you remove?
options: C) Burn or bury them away from the field
quiz.explanation: Burning or burying diseased leaves prevents spores from spreading back to healthy plants.

quiz.q: How much can pruning reduce fungicide sprays?
quiz.explanation: Pruning for airflow and removing diseased leaves can cut fungicide use by 30â50%.

quiz.q: What is the risk of over-pruning tomato plants?
quiz.explanation: Over-pruning exposes fruit to sunscald and reduces the leaf area needed for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: When is the best time of day to prune tomatoes?
options: A) Early morning when wet with dew
B) Mid-morning after dew has dried
quiz.explanation: Pruning when plants are dry helps wounds heal quickly and prevents disease spread.

quiz.q: What is a good disinfectant for pruning tools?
options: B) Bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water)
quiz.explanation: A 10% bleach solution kills most pathogens on tools.

quiz.q: How many main stems are commonly kept in a two-stem training system?
quiz.explanation: A two-stem system keeps the main stem and one strong sucker, balancing yield and airflow.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the Florida Weave method?
options: A) Tie twine to the first stake
quiz.explanation: Stakes are driven first to provide the structure for weaving twine.

quiz.q: Which of these is a determinate tomato variety?
quiz.explanation: Roma VF is a determinate variety that grows to a fixed height and fruits all at once.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pruning when plants are wet?
options: A) It is harder to see
quiz.explanation: Wet conditions help pathogens spread from plant to plant through pruning wounds.

quiz.q: How often should you check and repair trellises?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks ensure plants remain supported and prevent collapse after wind or rain.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of removing lower leaves?
options: A) It makes plants grow taller
B) It reduces soil-borne disease and improves airflow
quiz.explanation: Removing lower leaves prevents soil-borne fungi from splashing onto leaves and improves airflow.

quiz.q: How many stems are typically kept in a three-stem training system?
quiz.explanation: A three-stem system keeps the main stem and two strong suckers, often used in hot, dry areas.
